title: Stories on the Wall
sub: Grades 5–8 · Art · How Egyptian tomb painters told a story

hero.credit: Facsimile by Charles K. Wilkinson · The Met

objective: Students will look closely at copies of five tomb paintings from Thebes, made for The Met in the 1900s. They will find how the painters organized a wall (rows, a border, the background color), how one man is shown twice, and how small details carried meaning. Then they will design a two-row wall of their own, with one amulet symbol chosen for what it meant.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: These paintings were made more than three thousand years ago, yet we can still read them. Looking at how a painter organized a wall, and why, helps students make choices on purpose in their own work.

materials: Page 3 of this plan, projected or printed: three walls, and the symbols
Pencils, colored pencils (yellow, ochre, red, blue, green, black); differentiated handouts, one per student
connection: **Virtual visit:** open *Tomb Explorer* and find each wall’s three hidden details with the torch. Then *Build Your Own Tomb*: choose a wall, carve your name and lay your amulet in its niche.
**Design an Amulet** shows the symbols in this lesson, each with its meaning. Faience, a type of ceramic, was commonly used to make amulets.

steps.title: Who is in the boat?
script: Show the marshes wall and say nothing for a minute. Then ask students to count the people, and whether anyone appears twice. Someone will spot it: the tall man is there twice, raising a throwstick at birds on one side and spearing fish on the other. Only then name him: Menna. *“Menna fishes and hunts birds in the papyrus marshes, with his family crowded into his papyrus boat. The marsh teems with birds, fish, a crocodile and a small cat.”* Ask why a painter might show one man twice on one wall, and take ideas without settling it.

steps.title: Three ways to fill a wall
script: Show the three walls side by side. Students describe, then name: the harvest is in **two rows** (an art historian’s word is **register**); Sennedjem’s fields stack rows inside a **border of blue water**; Ipuy’s vineyard is one scene on a **yellow ground**. Ask what each choice does for a viewer.

groups.label: Two rows
groups.text: Harvest scenes, tomb of Menna, about 1396–1347 BCE. Above, surveyors in the grain; below, the chariot, the grain and the scribes.

items.caption: The harvest
items.alt: A tomb painting in two rows: above, men walk through a field of ripe grain holding a long rope; below, a horse and chariot wait while workers heap grain and scribes sit writing

groups.label: Rows inside a border
groups.text: Sennedjem and Iineferti in the Fields of Iaru, tomb of Sennedjem, about 1300–1224 BCE. The fields of the next world, ringed by water.

items.caption: The fields
items.alt: A tomb painting of fields bordered by blue water: a man and a woman cut grain, pull flax and plough with a pair of spotted cows, beneath a row of seated gods, with rows of date palms and flowers below

groups.label: One scene, a yellow ground
groups.text: Winemaking, tomb of Ipuy, reign of Ramesses II, about 1290–1224 BCE. From picking the grapes to treading them.

items.caption: The vineyard
items.alt: A tomb painting on a yellow ground: men pick bunches of dark grapes from a leafy vine into baskets, while others, holding ropes, tread grapes in a vat

steps.purpose: Compare how three painters organized a wall: two rows, rows in a border, one scene.
students: How many rows does each wall have?
What color is behind the figures?

steps.title: Details that carry meaning
script: Then the details. A painting could carry meaning in small things: the tilapia Menna spears were linked with new life, because they carry their young in their mouths; by defeating the wild creatures of the marsh, Menna was helping to keep the Egyptian world in order. In Sennedjem’s tomb a cat holding a knife is not a pet but a god: the sun god Ra, as a big tomcat who kills the snake of evil.

cells: With a long spear, Menna catches two large fish, most likely tilapia. Tilapia carry their young in their mouths, so they were linked with new life.
By defeating the wild creatures of the marsh, Menna was helping to keep the Egyptian world in order.
In chapter 17 of the Book of the Dead, the sun god Ra appears as a big tomcat who kills the snake of evil.
Here in the next world, the reaping is done not by farm workers but by Sennedjem and his wife themselves.
Two surveyors measure the field of grain with a rope knotted at regular spaces. Menna was in charge of the government’s lands.

steps.purpose: Learn what a few small details meant to the Egyptians.
students: Which detail is about the next world?

steps.title: These walls are copies
script: Last, the walls themselves. They are **facsimiles**: careful copies, in tempera on paper, most of them full size, made for The Met in the 1900s. Read Ipuy’s note: vineyards were usually painted on grey until the time of the kings called Ramesses, when painters began to use yellow.

screen.text:
These walls are copies: paintings in tempera on paper, most of them full size, made in the 1900s by artists working for The Met, of paintings in tombs at Thebes.
Vineyards were usually painted on a grey background, until the time of the kings called Ramesses, when painters began to use yellow, like this.

steps.purpose: Learn what a facsimile is, and see one choice painters changed over time.
students: Why would a museum make a full-size copy?
Why might a painter change the background color?

steps.title: Design your own wall
script: Students choose a handout. All three look closely at Menna’s wall first, then design a two-row wall about a day of their own, with one amulet symbol worked in for what it meant.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Find what Menna does on each side, match three details to what they tell us, choose a symbol, and draw a two-row wall with a guide for each row.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Compare the harvest’s two rows with Ipuy’s one scene, explain the yellow ground, plan each row, the symbol and the ground color, then draw.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Analyze how Menna’s wall is balanced around the papyrus, weigh what a facsimile can and cannot tell us, and design a wall that shows one person twice, with annotations.

steps.purpose: Look closely at Menna’s wall, then design a two-row wall of your own with one symbol, at the right level of challenge.
students: All three end with your own two-row wall and one symbol.

steps.title: Read a classmate’s wall
script: Partners swap walls and read each other’s, row by row, then name the symbol and guess why it was chosen before the artist explains. Two or three pairs share one choice that told them the most.

screen.question: Swap walls with a partner. Read their wall like an Egyptologist: what does each row show, and what does their symbol mean?

steps.purpose: Read a classmate’s design the way students read Menna’s wall.
students: What did your partner’s symbol mean, and why did they choose it?

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the objectives back on the screen, asked as questions: *“Can you now…?”* For each one, students show a thumb up, sideways or down. Ask one student to answer each aloud; for the last, ask a Red Level student, who explains why their wall shows one person twice.
